A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MMRole framework, dataset, agent and evaluator. Their main text, appendices, equations, tables and figures are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

before.justification: v1 reports original MMRole-Agent and baseline evaluations in Table 5, plus reward-model validation against GPT-4 and human judgments in Table 4.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds evaluator comparisons, visual-input and training-data ablations, prompt sensitivity tests and qualitative case studies.

M1.justification: The GPT-4-based data construction, QWen-VL-Chat fine-tuning, eight evaluation metrics and reference-relative reward-model scoring remain unchanged. The added multi-task explanation and quality-control details do not establish a changed procedure; the original generation, querying and scoring prompts are retained.

E1.justification: The same dataset, character populations, languages and three dialogue tasks remain, with unchanged statistics in Tables 1–2. Table 6 adds evaluation without visual input on the existing Out-Test tasks, extending coverage to an image-unavailable input condition.

E2.justification: The main comparator roster in Tables 3 and 5 is unchanged. Table 4 newly evaluates untuned QWen-VL-Chat as a judging baseline against the specialized reward model and GPT-4. Its previous participation as a role-playing agent did not cover this evaluator comparison.

E3.justification: v2 introduces several experimental protocols: GPT-4-scored Out-Test image-text relevance with and without images, one-epoch training on 8.5K versus 85K samples, character-subset training, and independent substitutions of two prompt components. Evaluator validation adds RMSE and Pearson metrics and assigns random scores when judging fails. The original splits and main training settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v1 lacks the controlled analyses added in Tables 6–8 concerning visual input, training-data quantity and character diversity. v2 also adds prompt sensitivity tests in Appendix L, further evaluator validation in Section 6.4 and Appendix J, and comparative case studies across both test splits in Appendix K.

E5.justification: v2 adds statistical reliability and agreement analysis through Cronbach's alpha in Section 6.4 and Pearson correlations in Appendix J. Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests; the four-human-evaluator validation design is retained.

E6.justification: Table 5's original scores remain identical, including MMRole-Agent's 0.994 overall score. Substantial new results include QWen-VL-Chat judging MAEs of 0.3780 against GPT-4 and 0.2439 against humans, image-text relevance of 0.9875 with images versus 0.7003 without for MMRole-Agent, and one-epoch full-data versus sampled-data scores of 0.989 versus 0.967. Additional validation, character-subset, prompt and case-study results are newly reported under their respective settings.

T1.justification: Section 3, Equation 1 corrects the dialogue history to end with the human utterance h_n instead of the target response m_n, removing circularity with Equation 2. The remaining mathematical formulation is retained, with no new theorem or proof.

C1.justification: The central claims remain the introduction of MRPAs, MMRole-Data, MMRole-Eval and the first specialized MMRole-Agent, together with improved performance and generalization. The added experiments support these existing contributions. The new GPT-4 dependence statement qualifies limitations without replacing the central claims.

C2.justification: Section 6.6 newly attributes generalization to data scale and character diversity, while Section 6.5 explains how dialogue history cushions the effects of removing images. Added discussions interpret evaluator consistency and prompt robustness. The conclusion identifies dependence on GPT-4-generated training data as a performance constraint, and Appendix A discusses simulated statements being mistaken for real individuals' speech.

D1.justification: v1 promises future release; v2 reports that data, code and models are available and that training/inference code and detailed evaluation results accompany the paper as supplementary materials. Table 3 adds model version dates, and Appendix F discloses character-profile checking and catchphrase verification. These materially expand documented reproducibility and access information; external availability was not independently verified.

R1.justification: v2 adds references including CharacterBox, AFlow, Qwen2-VL, LLaVA-OneVision, Improved Baselines with Visual Instruction Tuning, and Cronbach's reliability work. Related-work discussion is modestly updated, while the claimed positioning as the first multimodal role-playing framework remains unchanged. The retained Visual Instruction Tuning publication is matched across bibliographic updates.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are retained, with local copyediting and correction of 'four-fold' contributions to 'three-fold'. v2 adds Section 6.6, moves dialogue-filtering details into Appendix F, reorders prompt appendices and combines the two scoring-prompt sections. The changes constitute limited editing and reorganization alongside new scientific content.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 6–11 for ablations, evaluator validation and prompt sensitivity, plus six multi-panel case-study figures, Figures 14–19. Table 3 gains a version column, Table 4 gains comparator rows, and existing tables receive formatting changes. Retained prompt figures are relocated and renumbered, substantially expanding and reorganizing the evidence displays.

improvement.justification: v1 mainly supports the framework through benchmark scores and MAE-based evaluator validation. v2 addresses important evidential gaps with visual-input and training-data controls, an untuned evaluator baseline, and additional agreement and robustness analyses, while substantially improving reproducibility disclosures. The two prompt paraphrases support only narrow robustness, and repeated-run uncertainty remains absent. Nevertheless, the new evidence substantially strengthens the justification for the framework's central design choices without changing the original benchmark results.
